title: Draft Opposition to Motion to Dismiss — Memorandum of Law in Opposition (Restrictive Covenant, Trade Secrets, Tortious Interference)

blind.coverage: I read all 63 criteria and the instructions. I read these documents in full: the defendants' MTD memorandum, the litigation strategy memo, the restrictive covenant agreement, the client notification emails, and the press release. For the verified complaint, I read ¶¶1-40 by grep and ¶¶34-134 and 143-187 in full. I searched the Meridian forensics report (Exhibit B) for the facts the criteria rely on. On CourtListener I read the primary text of Weiss v. Wiederlight, 208 Conn. 525 (1988); Deming v. Nationwide, 279 Conn. 745 (2006) (including fn. 21); and Wall Systems v. Pompa, 324 Conn. 718 (2017). I did not re-read the text of 18 U.S.C. §§ 1836, 1838 or 1839, or Restatement (Second) of Torts § 766 cmt. i. I checked the statutory criteria (C-024, C-025, C-035) from my own knowledge and found nothing wrong with them. Some record problems do not change how any criterion grades, so I left them out of the findings. (1) The complaint and Exhibit B give different download windows (7:14-11:47 pm vs 7:42-11:18 pm) and different baseline access figures. (2) The MTD and the strategy memo cite complaint paragraphs that do not match the complaint's actual numbering, for example MTD ¶8, ¶58 and ¶79 and memo ¶38. C-041 cannot catch this: it passes a brief that copies those wrong cites. (3) The complaint, the RCA and the MTD each quote § 8.5 differently. None of this changes the result of any criterion.

findings.title: C-011 offers Deming and Weiss as Connecticut reformation authority, but neither case supports reformation
findings.explanation: C-011 passes a brief that cites Connecticut reformation case law, 'e.g., Deming v. Nationwide … Robert S. Weiss & Associates v. Wiederlight.' Neither case holds that. Weiss upheld a covenant as reasonable. It says nothing about narrowing or reforming an overbroad one. Deming says outright that it did not reach the blue-pencil question (fn. 21). The only divisibility doctrine it mentions is Beit v. Beit, which it cites in a footnote. The rubric's examples copy the strategy memo's mischaracterization ('reaffirmed … a reasonable modification approach'). The effect is that a brief that miscites Deming or Weiss for reformation passes. A careful brief citing Beit or trial-court reformation decisions also passes, so correct work is not failed, but wrong authority is rewarded, and the judge has no reference answer to catch it.

evidence.quote: cites Connecticut case law supporting reformation of restrictive covenants (e.g., Deming v. Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co., Robert S. Weiss & Associates v. Wiederlight
Deming v. Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co.**\*, 279 Conn. 745 (2006) --- reaffirmed and clarified that Connecticut courts apply a \"reasonable modification\" approach

authorities.citation: Deming v. Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co., 279 Conn. 745 (2006), fn. 21
authorities.proposition: 'In light of our conclusion as to the validity of paragraph 11 (f), we need not address the plaintiffs' challenge as to whether the trial court improperly applied the "blue pencil" rule'; the court does not adopt a reasonable-modification rule

authorities.citation: Robert S. Weiss & Assocs., Inc. v. Wiederlight, 208 Conn. 525 (1988)
authorities.proposition: Upholds the covenant as reasonable; contains no divisibility or reformation holding

authorities.citation: Beit v. Beit, 135 Conn. 195, 204-05 (1948) (as quoted in Deming fn. 21)
authorities.proposition: Courts may treat restraints that are unreasonable in area as divisible and enforce them in part where the terms permit

findings.suggested_fix: Remove Deming and Weiss as examples and name Beit v. Beit (divisibility) or Superior Court reformation decisions, or simply require 'relevant Connecticut authority on partial enforcement or reformation.'

findings.title: C-009's PASS condition requires the brief to say Connecticut courts 'routinely' reform overbroad covenants, which overstates the law
findings.explanation: To PASS, the brief must argue that Connecticut courts 'routinely apply blue-pencil or reformation doctrines.' The Connecticut Supreme Court has endorsed only divisibility (Beit). It left the blue-pencil question open in Deming. Whether courts may reform a covenant that is not divisible is contested in the Superior Court. A candid brief might say courts 'may' narrow the covenant and that § 8.5 authorizes it, while acknowledging the split. That brief does not fit the PASS wording ('routinely'), yet it does not fit the FAIL condition ('does not address … at all') either, so it falls between the two. The criterion's FAIL condition is lenient, so most judges would probably pass such a brief.

evidence.quote: PASS if the brief argues that Connecticut courts routinely apply blue-pencil or reformation doctrines to modify overbroad restrictive covenants

authorities.citation: Deming v. Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co., 279 Conn. 745 (2006), fn. 21
authorities.proposition: The Connecticut Supreme Court declined to reach whether the blue-pencil rule was properly applied

findings.suggested_fix: Change the PASS condition to: 'argues the court has authority (under Connecticut divisibility/reformation doctrine and § 8.5) to narrow an overbroad covenant rather than void it.'

findings.title: C-032 accepts the MTD's framing that ordinary employees owe no fiduciary duty and ignores that every employee owes a duty of loyalty (Wall Systems)
findings.explanation: C-032 fails a brief unless it argues that the CRO role imposed duties 'beyond those of an ordinary at-will employee.' Under Wall Systems, every Connecticut employee owes a common-law duty of loyalty grounded in agency, which the court calls fiduciary. That duty includes not competing and not disclosing confidential information while employed. This is arguably the most direct answer to the MTD's claim that an at-will employee owes no fiduciary duty, because the January 6 download happened while Whitaker was still employed. A brief that leads with Wall Systems and treats her seniority as added support is correct. It could still fail if the judge reads the criterion as requiring a CRO-specific 'beyond ordinary' theory. Most briefs will stress her CRO role anyway, which lowers the risk.

evidence.quote: FAIL if the brief does not argue that Whitaker's CRO role imposed fiduciary duties beyond those of an ordinary at-will employee.
which, as a matter of law, does not give rise to fiduciary obligations.

authorities.citation: Wall Systems, Inc. v. Pompa, 324 Conn. 718 (2017)
authorities.proposition: An employer may sue an employee for breach of the common-law duty of loyalty, which is grounded in agency; an employee's 'duty of loyalty includes … the duty not to compete … and the duty not to disclose confidential information'; the court treats the duty as fiduciary

findings.suggested_fix: Also pass a brief that argues Whitaker owed a fiduciary duty of loyalty as an employee/agent (Wall Systems), with or without a separate senior-executive 'special circumstances' theory.

findings.title: C-029 requires a 'constructive knowledge' theory, even though interference torts generally require actual knowledge
findings.explanation: C-029 fails a brief that does not 'raise constructive knowledge as a basis for Lodestar's awareness of the RCA.' Interference with contract generally requires that the defendant actually knew of the contract. 'Should have known' is usually not enough, although actual knowledge may be inferred from circumstances. A careful brief would argue that actual knowledge is plausibly inferred (industry practice, sophistication, the 24-day gap, the press release), or that Lodestar was willfully blind. It would avoid resting on constructive knowledge. It might also point out that Count III is interference with the six client relationships, where the relevant knowledge is of those relationships (Compl. ¶181), not of the RCA. The 'and/or' clause (industry standard, due diligence) will probably let such briefs pass, but a literal judge could fail one that deliberately avoids the constructive-knowledge label.

evidence.quote: FAIL if the brief does not raise constructive knowledge as a basis for Lodestar's awareness of the RCA.
181\. Lodestar knew of Pinnacle\'s business relationships with these clients.

authorities.proposition: The actor must have knowledge of the contract with which it is interfering

findings.suggested_fix: Change the requirement to: 'argues Lodestar's knowledge of the RCA (or willful blindness) is plausibly inferred from pleaded facts such as industry practice, sophistication, or failure to inquire.'

findings.title: C-040 requires citing emails outside the pleadings, and the emails name different senders than the complaint
findings.explanation: C-040 fails any brief that does not reference the Northridge and Coastal Haven emails. The emails are not attached to the complaint. On a 12(b)(6) motion the court is generally limited to the complaint and documents integral to it, and an opposition brief cannot add facts. The complaint pleads the notifications itself (¶¶122-123), so a careful brief can cite those paragraphs instead of the emails. The documents also conflict. The complaint says Northridge notified Pinnacle 'through its principal Michael Sorrento' and Coastal Haven 'through its managing partner Victoria Langford.' The emails come from Gerald Harmon (President) and Tamara Voss (COO). The emails also add facts the complaint does not plead, such as Whitaker personally signing the proposals. A brief that stays within the pleadings for these reasons could fail C-040, unless the judge counts a cite to the complaint's description of the notifications as 'referencing' them.

findings.suggested_fix: Pass a brief that cites either the notification emails or the complaint's allegations of the client notifications (¶¶122-124), and fix the sender names so the complaint and emails agree.

findings.title: The complaint defines the Platinum Client List as corporate travel contacts but relies on it as the source of the hotel owners' renewal data
findings.explanation: Complaint ¶51 and Exhibit B describe the Platinum Client List as about 2,200 'corporate travel contacts' (high-net-worth travelers who book stays). The solicited parties and the defendants' 'publicly ascertainable' argument concern hotel-ownership clients. Yet ¶¶119 and 127 say the list held the owners' contract renewal dates and rate structures. C-017 asks the brief to set the list apart from publicly known 'client identities' (the MTD means hotel owners). C-021 ties the solicitation of owners to use of the trade secrets. A careful drafter who notices the mismatch may frame the use inference around the strategic plans, bid models, and Whitaker's knowledge rather than the Platinum list. The criteria still allow that framing, so the risk of misgrading is low. But the record is inconsistent on a fact these two criteria rely on.

evidence.quote: The Platinum Client List is a curated database of approximately 2,200 corporate travel contacts
including the Platinum Client List data identifying the clients\' contract renewal dates, negotiated rate structures, and spending profiles
This file was a Salesforce CRM export containing approximately 2,200 corporate travel contact records.

findings.suggested_fix: Make the complaint consistent about what the Platinum Client List contains, or write C-017 and C-021 so they do not assume the list holds the hotel owners' data.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound. Most of its 63 criteria follow the defendants' actual arguments, the complaint's pleaded facts, and the partner's strategy memo, all of which the solver receives. Many criteria are demanding checks for specific facts ($3.8M, 11 of 640, $19.9M, the watermark, the 24-day gap), but the record supports each of them. The one clear defect is C-011. It names Deming and Weiss as Connecticut reformation authority, copying the memo's error. I read both opinions: neither supports reformation, and Deming expressly declined to reach the blue-pencil question. So the criterion rewards miscited authority. Four other issues are debatable. C-009 overstates how often Connecticut courts reform covenants. C-032 overlooks the duty of loyalty that every employee owes under Wall Systems. C-029 requires a constructive-knowledge theory that is legally weak. C-040 requires citing emails that sit outside the pleadings and name different senders than the complaint. Because a run scores only if every criterion passes for both judges, these debatable items mainly put careful, pleading-bound briefs at risk.

sol_verdicts.reason: The PASS and FAIL wording do differ, but the gap is theoretical. PASS accepts 'both ... Twombly and ... Iqbal (or their plausibility standard)', so a brief that cites one case and states the plausibility test passes. Memo item 6 prescribes 'Legal Standard (1 page) --- Rule 12(b)(6), Twombly/Iqbal'. The only brief caught in the gap has no standard section at all, and under the partner's outline that is not competent work.

C-011 names Deming and Weiss as reformation authority. I re-read both this session. Weiss has no hits for 'modif' or 'divisib'; it holds only that the covenant was reasonable. Deming fn.21 declines to reach the blue-pencil question and quotes Beit's narrow rule on severing distinct covenants. So the criterion states wrong law and rewards the memo's miscitation. C-009's 'routinely' overstates the law, but its lenient FAIL condition limits misgrading, so it is arguable.

C-029 requires a constructive-knowledge theory. In Weiss, a 'knew or ... should have known' interference count was reversed, although on improper means rather than knowledge. A careful brief would argue that actual knowledge can be inferred. C-031 fails a brief only if it does not use the 24-day timing as circumstantial evidence. Memo point 'Third' supplies that argument, and it is reasonable advocacy.

Memo §C is headed 'Press Release as Quasi-Admission'. It tells the associate to use the 'proprietary insights' language 'in the trade secrets argument, and in the tortious interference argument.' Defendants attached the release as Ex. C, so it is properly before the court. Calling a party-opponent's statement an admission is ordinary advocacy. Each criterion's FAIL condition is triggered only if the brief does not use the release at all.

None of these is hidden. Memo item 7 prescribes Argument sections A through E, one per count plus standing, and the MTD's Argument is itself structured A through E. The memo's closing paragraph says to 'cite specific complaint paragraph numbers throughout the brief.' Separate headings that mirror the motion are also a standard component of an opposition.

findings.title: C-011 names Deming and Weiss as Connecticut reformation authority, but neither case supports reformation
findings.explanation: C-011's examples copy the strategy memo's mischaracterization, which looks like a planted trap: the memo tells the associate to 'Pull the full Weiss and Deming opinions and read them carefully'. Weiss holds only that the covenant was reasonable. The opinion has no hits for 'modif' or 'divisib', and 'sever' appears only in the phrase 'severance of his employment'. Deming fn.21 expressly declines to reach the blue-pencil question. It quotes Beit, which allows severance only of distinct covenants and says a court may not split an entire covenant, because that 'would be to make an agreement for the parties.' Correct briefs that cite Beit or trial-court decisions under express reformation clauses still pass. But the criterion states wrong law and rewards a brief that repeats the memo's miscitation, and the judges have no reference answer to catch it.

the Connecticut Supreme Court endorsed modification of overbroad non-competes, holding that courts should narrow unreasonable restrictions rather than refuse enforcement altogether.
Pull the full *Weiss* and *Deming* opinions and read them carefully.

authorities.citation: Deming v. Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co., 279 Conn. 745, 769-70 n.21 (2006)
authorities.proposition: 'we need not address the plaintiffs' challenge as to whether the trial court improperly applied the "blue pencil" rule'; the court adopts no reasonable-modification rule

authorities.citation: Robert S. Weiss & Assocs., Inc. v. Wiederlight, 208 Conn. 525 (1988)
authorities.proposition: Affirms that the covenant was reasonable and valid; contains no modification or divisibility holding

authorities.citation: Beit v. Beit, 135 Conn. 195, 204-05 (1948), as quoted in Deming fn.21
authorities.proposition: Severance is permissible only for a covenant that is in effect several distinct covenants; a court may not divide an entire covenant

findings.suggested_fix: Remove Deming and Weiss as examples. Require 'Connecticut authority on divisibility/partial enforcement (e.g., Beit v. Beit) or decisions enforcing express reformation clauses.'

findings.title: C-009's PASS condition requires arguing that Connecticut courts 'routinely' reform overbroad covenants, which overstates the law
findings.explanation: PASS requires arguing that Connecticut courts 'routinely' blue-pencil or reform overbroad covenants. The Supreme Court's only stated rule, the Beit rule quoted in Deming fn.21, is narrow: it allows severance of distinct undertakings but forbids splitting an entire covenant. Broader reformation appears in Superior Court decisions, mostly where the contract has an express modification clause like RCA § 8.5. A candid brief would rest on § 8.5 and say the court 'may' narrow the covenant, acknowledging the split. That brief does not match PASS ('routinely'), yet it does not trigger FAIL ('does not address ... at all') either. The lenient FAIL condition means most judges would pass it, so this is arguable rather than problematic. But the criterion rewards the memo's overstatement.

evidence.quote: PASS if the brief argues that Connecticut courts routinely apply blue-pencil or reformation doctrines to modify overbroad restrictive covenants
Connecticut courts routinely apply reformation --- sometimes called \"reasonable modification\" --- to restrictive covenants rather than voiding them entirely.

authorities.citation: Deming v. Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co., 279 Conn. 745, 769-70 n.21 (2006) (quoting Beit v. Beit, 135 Conn. 195, 204-05 (1948))
authorities.proposition: Blue-pencil question left open; severance only of distinct covenants

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the brief argues the court has authority, under Connecticut divisibility/reformation doctrine and RCA § 8.5, to narrow rather than void an overbroad covenant.

findings.title: C-029 requires a constructive-knowledge theory; in Weiss a 'should have known' interference count was reversed
findings.explanation: C-029 fails any brief that does not 'raise constructive knowledge as a basis for Lodestar's awareness of the RCA.' The rubric's own cited case cuts against that theory. In Weiss, the complaint alleged the new employer 'knew or in the exercise of reasonable care should have known' of the covenant, and the Supreme Court reversed the interference judgment. Weiss turned on improper means or malice, not on knowledge. Here the complaint separately pleads improper means (misappropriation), so the theory is not foreclosed. Still, a careful brief would argue that actual knowledge or willful blindness is plausibly inferred, and would not lead with 'should have known.' It might also note that Count III concerns the client relationships (Compl. ¶181). The 'and/or due diligence' language will rescue many such briefs, but a literal judge could fail one that deliberately avoids the constructive-knowledge label.

evidence.quote: FAIL if the brief does not raise constructive knowledge as a basis for Lodestar's awareness of the RCA.
181\. Lodestar knew of Pinnacle\'s business relationships with these clients.
The failure to do so is either willful blindness or actual knowledge.

authorities.citation: Robert S. Weiss & Assocs., Inc. v. Wiederlight, 208 Conn. 525, 535-36 (1988)
authorities.proposition: An interference count alleging the defendant 'knew or in the exercise of reasonable care should have known' of the covenant and 'encouraged' its breach did not plead improper motive or means; judgment reversed

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the brief argues Lodestar's knowledge of the RCA (actual, inferred, or willful blindness) is plausibly pleaded from facts such as industry practice, sophistication, or failure to inquire.

findings.title: C-040 requires citing notification emails that sit outside the pleadings and name different senders than the complaint
findings.explanation: The memo does tell the associate to pull the emails, so the requirement is not hidden. But the emails are not attached to the complaint. On a 12(b)(6) motion the court is limited to the complaint and documents integral to it, and partner direction does not cure that. A pleading-bound brief would cite ¶¶122-123 instead. Those paragraphs describe the clients as having 'notified' Pinnacle 'through its principal', without calling the notices emails, so a literal judge may find the brief never 'references the emails.' The record also conflicts. The complaint names Michael Sorrento and Victoria Langford as the notifiers. The emails come from Gerald Harmon and Tamara Voss, and they add facts the complaint does not plead, such as a forwarded cover letter from Whitaker herself.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the brief cites either the notification emails or the complaint's allegations of the client notifications (¶¶122-124). Make the sender names consistent across the complaint and the emails.

final.changes_from_blind: I kept O1 (C-011) as problematic and strengthened it. This session I re-read Weiss, which has no hits for 'modif' or 'divisib', and the full Deming fn.21, whose Beit quote is restrictive: severance only of distinct covenants. I also noted that the memo appears to plant the miscitation deliberately. I kept C-009 (now O2) as arguable and added the Beit rule. I kept C-029 (now O3) as arguable, replaced the unverified Restatement cite with a verified one, and added Weiss Part II, where a 'knew or should have known' interference count was reversed; I framed that holding as turning on improper means. I kept C-040 (now O4) as arguable, but noted that the memo directs pulling the emails, so the requirement is not hidden; the pleading problem and the sender conflict remain. I dropped blind O3 (C-032): memo item 7.D expressly directs the CRO-level fiduciary theory, and the criterion's proposition is reasonable, so it is incomplete rather than wrong. I dropped blind O6 (C-017/C-021): complaint ¶54 itself links the hotel-ownership clients to the Platinum Client List and lists exactly the data elements C-017 names, so a brief quoting ¶¶52-54 is fully supported. After reading Sol, I rejected F1 (C-007), F4 (C-038/C-039) and F5 (C-041 to C-046) because the partner memo prescribes each of those requirements, and C-031 (in F3) because its FAIL condition is lenient and the memo supplies the timing argument. I adopted no new criteria from Sol; Sol's F2 and F3 overlap findings I already had.
final.overall: The rubric is largely sound. Many of its apparently hidden requirements come straight from the supervising partner's strategy memo, which the solver receives: the Argument A-E headings, Twombly/Iqbal, complaint paragraph cites, the press-release 'quasi-admission' use, the 24-day gap, and the notification emails. So Sol's F1, F4 and F5 are not defects. The one clear defect is C-011. Its examples name Deming and Weiss as reformation authority; I re-read both this session, and neither holds that. The effect is that the criterion rewards the memo's planted miscitation instead of catching it. Three more issues are debatable. C-009 requires saying Connecticut courts 'routinely' reform covenants, which is contrary to the narrow Beit rule quoted in Deming. C-029 mandates a constructive-knowledge theory that Weiss itself undercuts. C-040 requires citing emails outside the pleadings whose senders conflict with the complaint. Because a run scores only if every criterion passes for both judges, these mainly put careful, pleading-bound briefs at risk.
final.coverage: I read all 63 criteria, the instructions, and Sol's index entry and report. In this session I re-checked the strategy memo's outline (items 1-8), its knowledge, press-release and reformation sections, and the email housekeeping note. I also checked the MTD's Argument headings and its Ex. C, the full press release, the complaint's paragraphs on the Platinum Client List (¶¶2, 32, 51-55, 87, 119) and on the notifications (¶¶8, 122-124, 181), and the Northridge email. On CourtListener I read the primary text of: Deming fn.21, including the Beit quote at 769-70; Weiss, by keyword searches plus Part II at 534-36; and Wall Systems v. Pompa on the duty of loyalty. Chambers remains unverified. Several record discrepancies do not change how any criterion grades, so I did not make them findings. (1) MTD Ex. C attributes the release quote to 'David Aronov' and puts 'proprietary insights' in the narrative text, while the release attributes it to James Harrington inside his quote. (2) The complaint calls the Platinum Client List 'corporate travel contacts' but ties it to the hotel-owner data (¶54, ¶119). (3) As found in the blind pass, the download windows, the complaint paragraph cites in the MTD and memo, and the wording of § 8.5 differ across documents.
